main.title: Diddy Kong Racing
main.summary: Diddy Kong Racing is a 1997 kart racing game developed and published by Rare for the Nintendo 64.

cards.text: Diddy Kong Racing is a 1997 kart racing game developed and published by Rare for the Nintendo 64. The game revolves around Diddy Kong and his friends' attempt to defeat the intergalactic antagonist, a wizard pig named Wizpig, through winning a series of races. The player takes control of any of the featured characters throughout the game. Diddy Kong Racing features five worlds with four racetracks each, and the ability to drive a car, hovercraft, or pilot an aeroplane.

Development began after the release of Killer Instinct 2 (1996), and was intended to be an adventure game known as Wild Cartoon Kingdom in its early stages. As time progressed, the focus of development shifted from a Walt Disney World-influenced racing game to a unique title named Pro-Am 64, in which Nintendo had no involvement. Due to the delays of Banjo-Kazooie, Rare felt that they needed a stronger intellectual property to attract a wider audience for a game scheduled to release before Christmas 1997, thus making the decision to centre the game around Diddy Kong.

Diddy Kong Racing received critical acclaim upon release. The graphics, audio, and gameplay were among the most lauded aspects, while some criticism was directed at the game's repetition. It has sold 4.8 million copies since its release and stands as the Nintendo 64's eighth best-selling game. A sequel named Donkey Kong Racing was in development for the GameCube, but was abandoned in August 2002, one month before Microsoft purchased Rare for £375 million. An enhanced remake for the Nintendo DS titled Diddy Kong Racing DS was released worldwide in early 2007; it is the most recent Nintendo-published game to be developed by Rare.

main.title: Grand Theft Auto
main.summary: Grand Theft Auto is a 1997 action-adventure game developed by DMA Design and published by BMG Interactive.

cards.heading: Grand Theft Auto
cards.text: Grand Theft Auto is a 1997 action-adventure game developed by DMA Design and published by BMG Interactive. It is the first game in the Grand Theft Auto series and was released in November 1997 for MS-DOS and Windows, in December 1997 for the PlayStation and in October 1999 for the Game Boy Color. The game's narrative follows a criminal who climbs in status within the criminal underworld across three fictional cities, inspired by real-life locations. The gameplay is presented from a top-down perspective. It takes place within an open-world environment where the player must gather several points ranging in the millions to progress through the game's chapters. Points are gathered by completing various missions throughout each city, although the player can also gather points through other means.

cards.heading: Race 'n' Chase changes sides
cards.text: Grand Theft Auto began development as Race 'n' Chase, in which the player controlled a police officer pursuing criminals. However, the game was considered dull, and the concept of playing as a criminal was adopted. The development team worked to ensure that the player would have the freedom to play however they wanted. Grand Theft Auto created much controversy even before its launch due to its violent content, with discussions about banning its sale. The marketing campaign, organised by publicist Max Clifford, exploited this stirring of controversy as free promotion.

cards.heading: Reception and the London expansions
cards.text: Grand Theft Auto received mixed reviews but was a commercial success. While the graphics and controls were criticised, the entertainment value, sound design, and freedom of the gameplay were praised, and it has since been recognised as one of the greatest games of all time. Two expansions taking place in 1960s England, Grand Theft Auto: London 1969 and Grand Theft Auto: London 1961, were launched in 1999. The success of Grand Theft Auto spawned a series of games built upon the original's gameplay and themes; the Grand Theft Auto series has since become one of the most popular and best-selling video game franchises of all time. Grand Theft Auto 2 was released in October 1999.

cards.heading: A city seen from above, in 1997
cards.text: The first Grand Theft Auto presents Liberty City, San Andreas and Vice City from above the rooftops. Players answer telephones to accept jobs, earn points and build a multiplier while avoiding the police. Missions provide one route toward the score needed to progress, but the city also leaves room to pursue points through other activities.

main.title: Armored Core: Project Phantasma
main.subtitle: An earlier contract in the same world
main.summary: Armored Core: Project Phantasma is FromSoftware's second PlayStation mecha action game, first released in Japan on 4 December 1997. Set before the original Armored Core, it sends the mercenary pilot to investigate the Amber Crown complex and the research conducted there by the Doomsday Organization. An escaped prisoner, Sumika, becomes an ally while the rival pilot Stinger pursues them. The campaign gives this return to the workshop and battlefield a more concentrated storyline, keeping the first game's connection between paid missions, equipment and the machine assembled by the player.

cards.heading: An earlier contract in the same world
cards.text: Armored Core: Project Phantasma is FromSoftware's second PlayStation mecha action game, first released in Japan on 4 December 1997. Set before the original Armored Core, it sends the mercenary pilot to investigate the Amber Crown complex and the research conducted there by the Doomsday Organization. An escaped prisoner, Sumika, becomes an ally while the rival pilot Stinger pursues them. The campaign gives this return to the workshop and battlefield a more concentrated storyline, keeping the first game's connection between paid missions, equipment and the machine assembled by the player.

cards.heading: Bring a familiar machine into another campaign
cards.text: Save data from Armored Core can be imported, carrying a developed pilot and equipment into the new game. Additional weapons and parts expand the choices available in the garage. The underlying combat remains familiar, so a returning player can use knowledge of movement and equipment while responding to new missions. That continuity makes the sequel feel like another assignment within an established career. A build that worked before remains a starting point, but the player still has to decide whether its strengths suit the situation now being presented.

cards.heading: A rival on equal terms
cards.text: The new Arena mode gives the player another use for a customised Armored Core: a direct confrontation with another pilot. Away from a mission's changing objectives, the encounter concentrates attention on how two machines move and fight. It became a foundation for the next release, Master of Arena, where competitive rankings would take a larger role. Project Phantasma reached North America in 1998 but was not released in Europe. Within the original trilogy it supplies both a narrative prequel and an important addition to the series' structure of mercenary work.

main.title: The Last Blade
main.subtitle: Blades at the end of an era
main.summary: The Last Blade is SNK's weapon-based fighting game, first released for Neo Geo MVS in Japan on 5 December 1997.

cards.heading: Blades at the end of an era
cards.text: The Last Blade is SNK's weapon-based fighting game, first released for Neo Geo MVS in Japan on 5 December 1997. Its cast fights during the Bakumatsu period, drawing the setting's tensions together with supernatural imagery and Japanese mythology. Carefully staged backgrounds and restrained passages of music give the encounters a distinctive atmosphere. Before fighting, the player chooses between Power and Speed styles. That decision changes how the character can build attacks, placing a strategic preference alongside the choice of fighter before the first exchange has even begun.

cards.heading: Power or speed
cards.text: Power mode increases damage and provides access to particularly strong techniques under the necessary conditions. Speed mode allows normal attacks to link into longer sequences and special moves. The same character therefore supports different priorities: a player may seek a decisive opening or prefer to keep an opponent inside a connected series of strikes. Learning the chosen style means understanding both its opportunities and the situations in which it is vulnerable. The selection makes a return to a familiar fighter another chance to approach the round differently.

cards.heading: A reply inside the attack
cards.text: A dedicated deflection command lets the player answer an incoming attack and leave the opponent briefly open. Its timing gives defence a precise, active role within the weapon exchanges. The period setting also shapes the sound, with music drawing on orchestral textures suited to the nineteenth-century atmosphere. Hiroshi Yamazoe, Yasuhiro Naka and Yasuo Yamate contributed to the score. The Last Blade connects these measured surroundings to a combat system built around a small number of consequential choices: style, distance, commitment and the instant at which a strike can be turned aside.

main.title: Princess Crown
main.subtitle: The queen leaves the castle
main.summary: Princess Crown is Atlus and Sega's action role-playing game, first released for Saturn in Japan on 11 December 1997.

cards.heading: The queen leaves the castle
cards.text: Princess Crown is Atlus and Sega's action role-playing game, first released for Saturn in Japan on 11 December 1997. Gradriel, the young queen of Valendia, leaves her castle to help her people personally and becomes involved in a struggle against the demon lord Lalva. Side-view roads connect towns and dangerous areas, with expressive two-dimensional characters giving the journey the appearance of an illustrated tale. Director George Kamitani built an adventure in which talking, preparing supplies and fighting occupy different parts of the same small fantasy world.

cards.heading: Taking a breath between attacks
cards.text: Battles use direct attacks, dodges, shields and thrown weapons, with combinations produced through repeated inputs and movement. Each action consumes the Power gauge. Exhausting it leaves the character exposed, while walking or waiting allows it to recover. A successful exchange therefore includes a moment to withdraw as well as an opening to strike. Food and equipment support the journey between encounters: seeds can produce ingredients, and cooking turns those ingredients into more effective meals. Preparing something to eat becomes a practical part of surviving the next stretch of road.

cards.heading: Stories beyond one heroine
cards.text: Completing Gradriel's adventure opens scenarios for other characters whose paths intersect with hers. Playing those journeys extends the story towards its true ending, allowing another perspective on people already encountered. The game remained a Japanese release, but its detailed sprites and theatrical side-view scenes became influential in Kamitani's later work. Princess Crown preceded the founding of Vanillaware and the creation of Odin Sphere. Its lasting identity comes from the relationship between that visual storytelling and the physical rhythm of combat, where even a powerful heroine needs time to regain her breath.

main.title: Shining Force III
main.summary: The Saturn tactical RPG follows three armies through one political crisis, with grid battles, growing friendships and choices carried between scenarios.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Shining Force III is a tactical role-playing game developed by Camelot for Sega Saturn. The series' turn-based army battles move into a 3D world, with a story released across three scenarios in Japan during 1997 and 1998. The Western edition contains the first scenario, led by the young commander Synbios.

cards.heading: An army, one turn at a time
cards.text: A peace conference collapses into an abduction and a struggle between the Republic of Aspinia and the Destonian Empire. Synbios must move his allies through the fighting that follows. On the battlefield, each character advances across a grid and then attacks, casts a spell or uses an item. A powerful fighter stranded beyond the healer's reach can become a liability. Keeping the commander alive matters as much as reaching the next enemy, so a formation has to serve several needs at once.

cards.heading: The people behind the formation
cards.text: Between battles, the commander walks through towns, speaks to residents and equips the group for the journey ahead. The soldiers develop individually through experience, new spells and class promotions. They also build friendships by fighting together, gaining benefits when trusted companions remain close in battle. That gives the army a history beyond its equipment: characters who have supported one another can become useful partners on the map, and choosing where they stand helps preserve the relationship's practical advantage.

cards.heading: Three views of one conflict
cards.text: The three scenarios follow Synbios, Prince Medion and Julian through overlapping parts of the crisis. Japan received the first on 11 December 1997, the second on 29 April 1998 and the third on 23 September 1998. Saved progress can pass forward, allowing earlier decisions to affect later events. Scenes encountered from one army's position acquire another context when the next commander reaches them. Only Scenario 1 received an official English release; the other two complete the story in their Japanese Saturn editions.

main.title: Time Crisis II
main.summary: Time Crisis II is a 1997 light-gun shooter video game developed and published by Namco for arcades.

cards.text: Time Crisis II is a 1997 light-gun shooter video game developed and published by Namco for arcades. It is the second installment in the Time Crisis series. The game incorporates the same mechanics of its predecessor, with some minor changes, but with the addition of co-operative two-player gaming. The game's story focuses on the efforts of two secret agents, Keith Martin and Robert Baxter, as they attempt to thwart the efforts of an industry mogul's plan for world dominance.

The game was ported to the PlayStation 2 in October 2001, as part of a bundle to coincide with the launch of the GunCon 2 controller (G-Con 2 in Europe), with enhanced graphics. A port for the Dreamcast was cancelled during development. The game received mostly favorable reviews for the arcade and console versions. A sequel to the game, Time Crisis 3, was released in 2003.

main.title: Grandia
main.summary: Grandia is a role-playing video game developed by Game Arts and published by Entertainment Software Publishing for the Sega Saturn console as the first game in their Grandia series.

cards.heading: From Saturn to PlayStation
cards.text: Grandia is a role-playing video game developed by Game Arts and published by Entertainment Software Publishing for the Sega Saturn console as the first game in their Grandia series. Released in Japan in 1997, the game was ported to the PlayStation in 1999, with an English version of the game appearing on the platform in North America in the following September by Sony Computer Entertainment, and in Europe in 2000 by Ubisoft. The game was produced by much of the same staff who worked on the company's previous role-playing endeavor, the Lunar series, including producer Yoichi Miyagi and composer Noriyuki Iwadare.

cards.heading: Spin-offs and an HD return
cards.text: Grandia's combat mechanics have been carried over to future games within the franchise. The game has also spawned an expansion disk (Grandia: Digital Museum) and a spin-off title (Grandia: Parallel Trippers) - both released exclusively in Japan. In celebration of the renewed development on Grandia Online, which acts as a prequel to Grandia, the game was re-released on Sony's PlayStation Network platform in 2009. A high-definition remaster of the game and its sequel, Grandia II, was released for Nintendo Switch in August 2019, and for Windows in October 2019. PlayStation 4 and Xbox One versions were released in March 2024.

cards.heading: Justin and the lost civilisation
cards.text: The game is set in a fantasy world of emerging technology and exploration. A young boy named Justin inherits a magic stone that leads him on a journey around the world to uncover the mystery of a long-lost civilization. Along the way, he meets other adventurers who join him on his quest, which draws the attention of the militaristic Garlyle Forces who seek to uncover the secrets of the past as well. Grandia received a largely positive critical response during its original release, and was voted by readers of the Japanese magazine Famitsu as the 73rd greatest game of all time in a 2006 poll.

main.title: Mega Man Legends
main.summary: Mega Man Legends is a 1997 video game released by Capcom.

cards.text: Mega Man Legends is a 1997 video game released by Capcom. It is the first game in the Mega Man Legends sub-series of Mega Man games from Capcom, and the second major 3D polygonal Mega Man title in the franchise, following Mega Man: Battle & Chase. It was released for the PlayStation in 1997 in Japan, and in 1998 in North America. A Nintendo 64 port was released in 2000 with the same title, but it was renamed Mega Man 64 for the North American release in 2001. It was also ported to Windows in 2001, and to the PlayStation Portable in 2005, the latter only in Japan. Its most recent release was as a PS one Classic on the North American PlayStation Network in 2015.

Legends stars a new incarnation of Mega Man, known as Mega Man Volnutt, the game's player character. Mega Man Volnutt is a "Digger", someone tasked with investigating ruins on a flooded Earth. During his journey with his friends, their ship crashes on Kattelox Island, where Mega Man confronts pirates seeking the island's hidden treasure. As an action-adventure game, Mega Man Legends's gameplay is significantly different from the original series, though it retains some familiar elements.

Mega Man Legends received positive critical reception for its transition from 2D graphics to 3D. However, the Nintendo 64 and Windows ports were criticized for lacking improvements over the PlayStation version, and their graphics were considered outdated by the time of their release. Mega Man Legends was followed by the prequel The Misadventures of Tron Bonne and the sequel Mega Man Legends 2.

main.title: Gran Turismo
main.subtitle: A driving career begins with an affordable car
main.summary: On December 23, 1997, Gran Turismo was released in Japan on PlayStation after roughly five years of development.

cards.heading: The first Gran Turismo
cards.text: Gran Turismo was released in Japan for PlayStation on December 23, 1997, after roughly five years of development. Kazunori Yamauchi's driving game combined vehicle physics, engine sounds and detailed car models with a career of races and upgrades. Its catalogue included more than one hundred models and eleven circuits, giving players production cars to learn, collect and improve.

cards.heading: Parameters and accessible handling
cards.text: Yamauchi described a physics engine using detailed parameters drawn where possible from real-car design data or measurements. Different vehicles were meant to respond according to their own characteristics. Tests also showed many players entering corners too quickly and crashing. The team worked to make handling more accessible while retaining the simulation, helping players understand how each car reacted.

cards.heading: A career built on credits and upgrades
cards.text: In Gran Turismo Mode, race winnings become credits for cars and parts. Upgrades can make more demanding events possible, so an affordable first vehicle can remain useful as the player improves it. Yamauchi linked this progression to computer RPGs such as Wizardry and Ultima. Managing purchases and developing a car accompany the improvement of driving skills.

cards.heading: Learning the differences between production cars
cards.text: The official record describes more than one hundred models and 146 variants. Alongside faster machinery are production cars recognisable from ordinary roads. Their differing power, weight, drivetrain and setup give players reasons to compare them. Driving several versions of a familiar car can reveal handling differences that are less apparent from appearance alone.

cards.heading: Reflections and replays
cards.text: Yamauchi recalled the team's excitement at seeing a car rotate in real time with convincing reflections. PlayStation's limited geometry and texture resources required careful choices in shading and surface detail to convey paint, metal and glass. Replays then presented the vehicles through cinematic camera positions, letting players observe the cars as well as control them.

cards.heading: A small team over five years
cards.text: Yamauchi and Shuhei Yoshida recalled five people at the beginning and fewer than twenty even toward the end. The team spent about five years developing physics, graphics, car data and content together. Yamauchi worked on the idea while making Motor Toon Grand Prix, gaining experience and internal support. Gran Turismo's success later helped establish Polyphony Digital as an independent studio.

cards.heading: The Japanese launch
cards.text: Yamauchi remembered visiting major shops on the Japanese launch day, December 23, 1997, and seeing people queue for the game. The series' official page identifies the first release as the beginning of the Real Driving Simulator. Its success provided a foundation for a larger sequel and an expanding relationship with the automotive industry.
